item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports separating recency, order, and history aggregation. RecSys 2024’s [Does It Look Sequential?](https://doi.org/10.1145/3640457.3688195) uses sequence shuffling across 15 datasets, finding weak sequential structure in several popular benchmarks. [Measuring Recency Bias](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) (2024) proposes a dedicated recency metric and reports improvements from mitigating excessive recent-item emphasis. A [2026 Spotify study](https://research.atspotify.com/2026/10/do-sequential-recommendation-benchmarks-require-higher-order-sequence-modelling) finds pairwise transition models outperform reproduced SASRec/eSASRec on four of five benchmarks: strong rankings need not demonstrate higher-order sequence understanding. [SIGIR 2026 research](https://doi.org/10.1145/3805712.3809738) uses controlled perturbations to diagnose middle-position neglect, motivating position-aware probes beyond attention inspection.\n\nPractical synthesis: compare original histories with recent-only truncation, recent-block removal, isolated-old-item removal, and repeated-interest-group removal. Shuffle earlier interactions while fixing the last item to separate order dependence from last-item reliance. Match removal controls by interaction count, training-item popularity, and position; define interest similarity using available titles/descriptions or training co-occurrence. Keep candidates fixed within each pair; report target-rank change, top-10 overlap, score-margin change, and paired HR@10 differences, with user-level bootstrap intervals and repeated shuffle seeds. For SASRec, accompany rankings with final-representation cosine changes and comparisons against last-item and recency-weighted pooling baselines. These are proposed diagnostic controls, not a standardized protocol established by the cited papers. Large effects identify model sensitivity; they do not establish user intent, preference shifts, or causal interest. Use patterns to motivate validation-tested changes to recency weighting, position handling, aggregation, or training objectives."}
